stories.title: The Pro-AI Narrative
stories.about: Build the machines that arm artists
stories.blurb: A pro-AI case for building instruments that help artists explore, test, and distribute their work without turning the machine into the artist.
stories.transcript: I've entered us in a competition! For what? Building things with artificial intelligence! There's even a prize for going viral! How does one go viral? That's what we're going to find out. Build us a way for artists to share competing versions of their work so audiences can help them choose what to publish. Use what we already have. Show me what works, what doesn't, and what it costs. There. Now it builds! Well, we do what? Discuss the future! I've been researching virality. It appears to be a system for distributing information through people. Does it distribute money? Not necessarily. Then why are we competing? Because artists need audiences. Artists need customers. They need to find the people who care about what they make. Which raises a question. Is going viral valuable because many people see something or because the right people see it? One million people watching me starve is not a business model. Exactly! What if the million people watching could help you find the hundred who would pay to keep you creating? Then attention becomes a search mechanism. Provided it eventually finds a wallet. There's another problem. Many artists fear machines will replace them. Then we're building the wrong machines. Ours is building something right now. Yes, but it's not making art to compete with us. It's building instruments we can use. Like a paintbrush? An energy paintbrush! You bring an idea. The machine helps you explore it, produce it, test it and find a market. And if the machine becomes the artist? Then we've lost the point. I want artists to own their tools, choose their methods and keep their audiences. Even change the machines themselves? Especially that. We're starting with Meta's models. Next, we'll see what can run locally, what can be open source and what we can replace without losing the art. So this isn't a competition to build the best artist? It's a competition to build a better paintbrush. Leonardo, the machine has finished. Did it work? The acceptance tests passed. Here is the evidence. And the cost? Some costs are recorded. Some remain unknown. At least it's learning to tell the truth. Good. Then we know what to improve tomorrow. But we still haven't gone viral. Maybe we shouldn't try to make the machine famous. What should we make famous? The artists who use it. If you're an artist, tell us what tool you wish existed. Help us build it, help us test it, then make something the world hasn't seen. And sell it! Arm the artists. Your energy paintbrush. Not your market competition.
stories.source_text:
@Meta @Steph_Curdy This video is the demo of the actual product in use.

It's the main one I submitted for the hackathon.

It shows the baseline view of how AI can run in the background and produce trusted outputs.

While the characters use the time its working to explore possible futures. https://t.co/GODh48nW2C

stories.title: The Annalea Co-Founder Narrative
stories.about: Offer support without deciding for her
stories.blurb: A proposal to help a founder make the work around her research less consuming—while leaving the destination, terms, and decision with Annalea.
stories.transcript: Borges, another person wants more computers! Are you sure? Look! A founder explaining why she wants to leave her company. Her name is Annalia Layton. Wonderful! We should give her a human OS laptop. She says she already has access to essentially unlimited compute. That's an inconvenient fact for your laptop giveaway. Then what does she need? She's exhausted by the responsibilities of being a founder. She says she'd rather work for an AI lab. Buh. Yes? Isn't she already running an AI lab? Let's find out. Vext Labs, an independent AI research laboratory. Founded by? Annalia Layton. Borges! Yes? She already has the lab! Having a lab and wanting to operate a company are two different things. Then perhaps we're asking the wrong question. She also reports that her work has been seen by a million people in two days. A million? That's what she reports. Agno, put a million dollars in the ledger. Under what account? Annalia. That's not an account. A million people saw her work. Surely she's worth at least a million dollars. A million views do not establish a million dollar valuation. Why not? Because reach isn't revenue. Revenue isn't profit. And profit isn't the entirety of a person's potential economic contribution. Then what do the views prove? Assuming the reported reach is accurate, that her work attracted substantial attention. But nobody has to pay to look. Exactly. Then we don't know how much anyone is willing to pay for what she knows. Perhaps that's the problem. Which problem? A million people can see someone without any of them having a way to finance the work they want that person to do. That's a hypothesis. Not every viewer is a customer, employer or patron. Then we should find the people who are. Leonardo, before proposing anything, we ought to understand her work. What has she made? Six publicly listed research papers, each with a DOI. Six? The central theme is verified capability growth in AI systems. Capability growth? Instead of relying exclusively on making a large model bigger, her research investigates adding capabilities while preserving existing ones. A growing machine! With explicit checks. That sounds familiar. It should. Human OS also accumulates capabilities. At a different level. Our work concerns software capabilities around a person's operating environment. Her papers explore mechanisms for changing model architectures and evaluating whether their capabilities actually improved. So we are working on related questions at different layers. Precisely. What happens if we combine the layers? That's a question for a future experiment, not a conclusion. An experiment with a budget. Naturally. Her research isn't merely a collection of predictions. Then what is it? A proposed mechanism for growing models, paired with tests that limit what can honestly be claimed about the results. Tell me more. One of her papers is called the accretion model. Accretion? Like layers of sediment? Or adding something new without overwriting everything beneath it. So learning something new shouldn't require forgetting something old. That's the design aspiration. The reported demonstrations have defined limits. And the other papers? She explores verifier-gated improvement, mechanisms for injecting capabilities, and how to distinguish genuine progress from results contaminated by leakage. That last one is extremely important. Why are you shouting? Because I have repeatedly been accused of celebrating results that don't prove what their inventors think they prove. And this research takes that problem seriously. Wonderful! I have notes! On her public research list, ideas that failed stay on the list. Failures? Ideas her own tests proved wrong. One paper is a record of them. And she published them? Yes. She kept the failures! Their evidence about which approaches didn't succeed under the tested conditions. Borges, that's foresight! In what sense? She's building a way to know where the future growth is real before asking the world to trust the claim. That's a fair description of the research direction. Not proof that it has already solved frontier scale model improvement. And now she wants to join one of the labs with the resources to explore it further. According to her post, yes. Then perhaps the labs should be looking at her papers. They certainly can evaluate them. I've discovered why her work interests me. Go on. Everyone is trying to make the machines more capable. Many researchers are. But how do we know they actually became more capable? Through carefully designed evaluation. And what happens when the tests themselves are incomplete? We need to recognize the limits of the evidence and design better tests. So her research is not just about making models grow. It's also about making claims of growth inspectable. And she has another project! Jewel. What's jewel? A human-directed AI product. Users can converse with it, maintain controlled memory, use developer interfaces and approve certain actions before they occur. Human intent, approval, memory, records. Familiar themes. Borges, perhaps she's looking at the same future from another direction. The projects have meaningful conceptual overlap. We shouldn't assume their implementations are interchangeable. But we can explore whether they fit. With her consent. Of course. And with clear rights to the work, data, intellectual property and resulting capabilities. I haven't even invented the partnership yet. Then this is an excellent time to avoid inventing its liabilities. There's another post. Another paper? No. She says her house has flooded. She shares a video of the situation. After all that? The physical world doesn't stop making demands because someone is conducting important research. She has six papers, an AI product and people paying attention to her work. Yes. And she still has to deal with everything outside the laboratory. Yes. Borges, what does unlimited compute do about that? Some useful tasks can be delegated to computers. Other burdens require money, practical help, human relationships or rest. Then perhaps she doesn't need us to give her another agent. Perhaps not. She needs fewer things demanding that she becomes someone else in order to keep doing the research. We can't determine her needs from a few posts. But we can ask what support she would actually find useful. That's the right starting point. Somebody call for a ride? We have discovered a founder who would rather work for an AI lab. And? She already founded one. Well, isn't that something? I want to be her co-founder. Does she want a co-founder? I don't know. Then you've discovered a question, not a partnership. We could offer co-founder style support as an optional arrangement. We could help with the work surrounding the research. What work? Finding collaborators, presenting her research, managing experiments, connecting potential sponsors, identifying opportunities and making the business side less consuming. Without changing the research claims or presenting a proposed feature as a shipped result. And without assuming she wants to continue operating Vex Labs. Yes! She could pursue a lab position if that's what she wants. There you go. Don't make your solution another job she has to manage. Then what do we call it? Didn't you invent something for this? An art-up. A structure intended to support a creator's work while allowing other people and systems to contribute capabilities, funding and distribution. The proposed model still needs a sustainable business, clear agreements and real funding. Yes. But we can invite her to test the idea with us. Now you're talking. I still think she should be worth a million dollars. Worth to whom? To the AI labs. Then find out what they need, what they would pay for and what she would actually accept. But look at all the work she's done. That gives us concrete evidence of research interests, technical artifacts and methods. It does not automatically establish the monetary value of an employment contract or acquisition. Then let's ask the market. How? We make a beautiful, evidence-backed presentation of her work. With citations to the papers and their actual limitations. We show the frontier questions her research could help address. We provide continual capability growth, reproducible evaluations, safeguarding against false improvement claims and human-authorized agent systems. And we invite qualified labs to compete to support that work. With her permission. And without inventing competing offers. Then they can offer her a role. Or funded research collaboration, depending on what she wants. Or support her independent lab. These are different transactions. Each needs its own terms. And if the combined offers reach a million dollars? Then you'll have a much better basis for discussing a million dollar opportunity. So the million views aren't the price? No. They're what made us look. And the work is what gives us something worth examining. I like that better. Alright, what's the destination? Annalia Layton. Vex Labs. What's the cargo? An episode about her research. A sourced summary of the technical work and why it may interest Frontier AI Labs. A proposal for a bounded collaboration, not an unrequested takeover of her company. And the question? Would she like help making the work of being a founder less consuming while she decides whether to pursue employment, independent research or both? Good. We can bring the art up. If she wants it. We can find patrons. If they agree to fund the work. We can tell the labs what she's built. If she approves how we represent her and her research. Now, suppose she says she'd still rather go work for a lab. Then we help the right lab discover her work. And if she doesn't want our help at all? Then she doesn't have to take it. Well now, you've finally invented a ride with a door that opens from the inside. Leonardo, there's something interesting about Annalia's research. What? An idea that verified improvements might accumulate without destroying what came before. Yes. You've been trying to do something similar for human productive capabilities. The computer remembers what it learned to build. And can reuse it later. But there's something else. What? A human has accumulated capabilities too. Yes. Research, judgment, experience, failed experiments, ideas that might become useful later. Yes. When they join a new company, we sometimes treat them as though the most important thing they bring is their ability to operate someone else's machine. Companies can also value the expertise they bring. The question is how that expertise is recognized and supported. But what if we help the person carry their accumulated work into every new opportunity? With appropriate ownership, confidentiality and portability. Then joining a lab wouldn't have to mean forgetting everything they were building before. And staying independent wouldn't have to mean doing every job alone. Not if the support network is genuinely useful and economically sustainable. Then that's our invitation. Annalia has been investigating how a machine can gain new capabilities without losing its past. Yes. I want to help build a world where the human doesn't have to lose hers. Borges? Yes? What if the labs don't understand why they should be interested? Then we should make the relevant evidence easier to evaluate. And if they do understand? They can decide whether to make an offer. And if Annalia says no? Then she gets to decide what happens next. That's what the bus is for, honey. Getting possibilities to people. Not choosing their destinations for them. Agnolo? Yes? Do we have a million dollars yet? No. Then I suppose we'd better make something worth paying for. That was wonderful! I have notes! And for once, we might have someone interested in reading them. Borges, what qualifications does a co-founder need? That depends on the company. I can design machines? Yes. Make paintings? Yes. Write songs? Yes. Invent new businesses? Frequently. What else? Can you reliably reduce the founder's workload? That's the interview.
stories.source_text:
What if we bring someone in who recently had a million views to comment?

@annalea_l - you want to work at one of the frontier labs.

I have a frontier lab in the future.

I took one look at your site and immediately recognized why @jessyka_boat told me I should reach out to you and see if you were interested in being my cofounder.

I can't pay what the labs can. But I can tell the market what price I see on your work, and compress it for them to be able to bid on.

I'm putting a public value of $1M on your work because I know what it showcases. It's very close to my own.

Maybe the market can pay you $1M for me, then you don't have to join a big lab just for the cash.

I'll just try to hyperstition the grant for you.

And offer my services (and more importantly, the services of my cast) as your cofounder.

Just tell me anything you are having trouble with and I'll see what I can do with it.

My system grows the capabilities it needs to make every solution easier in the future and now that we are able to explain complex ideas in dialogue, I'm confident in the success of it.

I just need users who aren't blinded by the marketing hype of the big players with all the cash.

Hope you enjoy your movie Annalea.

Here to help if you don't want to give up on your lab quite yet.

Or help you secure your bag at the existing labs.

Regardless, you're too talented to be poorer than those buried in the depth of the labs.

Let's give the market a way to correct itself.

stories.title: The Arm the Artists Narrative
stories.about: Fund the people who keep the circle alive
stories.blurb: A grant, a financial report, and a long chain of labor: credit travels through the people who kept Vibecamp alive.
stories.transcript: Mail for the station. Good news, for once. Read it, Borges! Brooke Bowman writes, Vibecamp has been awarded a $300,000 grant from Lightcone Commons. $300,000! To artists! To Vibecamp. People who build a gathering in the woods for internet weirdos. Artists! I'll allow it. Agnolo! I said, arm the artists with money and let them cook. And now the artists are armed! When did you say it? It's on the monitor! Leo's post. This makes me so happy. Vibecamp is doing so much good for the world and it should be a lot easier for them. November 4th, 1116 in the morning. A quote of her post. Yes! And her post? November 2nd, 252 in the afternoon. So the money was awarded before you cheered for it? By about two days. 44 hours. And who gave it? Lightcone Commons. Everyone who built the grant program and everyone who contributed to it. And who did the work that earned it? The Vibecamp team. For years. She says they often had to pause paychecks, which were small to begin with, to make sure the organization could pay its bills. Could I claim credit for the cooking? The cooking hasn't started. For the Vibe, then? Ronaldo, the Vibe is the one thing nobody can claim. And you've been there. I have? Leo has. It was Vibecamp's fourth year and the first one on his radar. He wrote about it. What I learned from spending four days in the woods with a bunch of internet weirdos. Who paid for that? A grant. From Defender and the Open Research Institute. So before anyone armed the artists, somebody armed Leo. That's different! Is it? Less different than I hoped. The organizers opened with a session. Three things to practice. Saying and accepting yes. Saying and accepting no. And responding graciously. Whether or not the answer was what you'd hoped for. Responding graciously. Even when the answer is, it wasn't you. Especially then. What else did he learn? An improv session. Not improv for learning how to act. Improv for learning how to show up as yourself. They stood in a circle and passed an imaginary object around. It didn't exist except in the minds of the people in the circle. An object that only exists between people. And before you sent it, you had to catch someone's eyes. Make sure you had their attention. Then pass it. And they changed it and passed it on. Sometimes back to him. Sometimes to everyone else. Borges. Credit is the object in the circle. Go on. It doesn't belong to anyone. It only exists between people. If I grab it and hold on to it, the game stops. And if you pass it on? It changes. And it comes back bigger. That's the first accurate thing you've said about credit all week. Leo's essay ends with a post from Defender. No one really wants to save the world. What we want is to be given a role in saving it. So I didn't really want the $300,000. You did a little. A little. But mostly I wanted a role. Leo found his. He wrote that his role is the coordinator. Making sure the people working on saving the world can see each other. Then our role today is simple. We see them. Then let's celebrate. The artists are finally being recognized. Finally! What will they do with it? She says the focus will be internal for now rather than physical event infrastructure. Paying people enough that they don't risk burnout. Good. And training budgets. Especially for their safety council who do difficult mediation and support people who have experienced trauma. They're arming the people who protect the circle. She also says that at the last Vibe Camp, so many tickets sold at the last minute that she thought it might be the last one. And now? Now they have breathing room. A real chance to see what they can do with proper resources. There's one more thing in the thread. What? Even before the grant, they had started a thorough financial report. Costs and revenue over the years. Published within about a month. Agnolo, are you crying? It's a financial report, Leonardo. Of course I'm crying. Agnolo, put it in the ledger. Entry. Grant. $300,000. From Lightcone Commons to Vibe Camp. Earned by the Vibe Camp team over years. Credit claimed by Future Radio. None. Enjoy? Unlimited. It doesn't need an account. Any reply going out, honey? Just one. Thank you, Lightcone Commons. Congratulations, Vibe Camp. And thank you to everyone who passed the object along the way. Arm the artists with money. And let them cook. Agnolo, when they publish the financial report... Yes? Could there be a line for inspired by Leonardo? No. A footnote? Leonardo. Yes, yes. Pass the object.
stories.source_text:
the artists are being armed. Congrats to @gptbrooke and the @vibecamp_ team for the grant from https://t.co/P6pRZTZWAR

I had the pleasure of attending VC4, and wrote about it here: https://t.co/ch8zWi0Ukx

I submitted the event to Future Radio, and Leonardo tried to take credit for the grant. 

Which gave us a perfect chance to spread credit around to show where all the magic was being created.

#ArmTheArtists

stories.title: The Attend the Bloom Party Narrative
stories.about: Ask to enter the pro-future room
stories.blurb: A film about asking Tenso whether Future Radio can attend a tentative San Francisco gathering built against doomer narratives.
stories.transcript: From Tenso, at Distributed KV, November 2nd. Everyone is invited at the Bloom Party in SF, and we will not send you back, because that would be doomer behaviour. Even doomers are welcome to join this party. An invitation the host has promised not to take back. I've never seen terms like it. Then it's settled. We're going. Nothing is settled. We haven't asked. Then let's find out who we'd be asking. Tenso, San Francisco. His bio reads, Those who believe in power of memes rule the universe. September 20th. I wish we could cure all types of cancer tomorrow. I wish I never had to age. That's why I am not a doomer. That's the whole philosophy in three wishes. Then he started a group chat. Its purpose? Refuse and reject doomer narratives. Pro-tech, pro-future, pro-humanity. October 6th, 540 members, 300,000 messages, and 300 more people waiting to get in. 300,000 messages. In how long? Not long enough for anyone to have read them all. October 7th, he made it official. The anti-doomer non-movement. Sign in with X to join as a founding member. He spells it M-E-M-E-B-E-R. Memobas, because they believe in the power of memes. That same day, Leo posted, I'm a simple unk. When I see a non-movement that is anti-doomer, I sign up. So, he is a founding member of a movement that insists it isn't one. Booked. By October 18th, 750 members. Bloom, never doom. There's a second package. Smaller. The label says, some things are easier said anonymously. October 15th, Tenso launched unsaid. Sign in with X, get a link, and anyone can send you the thing they've never told you. The sender stays hidden from everyone, even the person who receives it, even the company. And the rules? Senders must be 18. No hate, no threats, no harassment, no one else's private information. Abuse is removed, and senders can be blocked. Good. A confession box with a bouncer. Two days later, Leo posted his own link. Hit me. Don't leave it unsaid. I have a confession. It's anonymous. Everyone in this room knows it's you. I want to go to the party. That isn't a confession, dear. That's an RSVP. October 26th. Super excited to introduce the first anti-doomer bloom party in SF. For the members. And for people who believe in a truly abundant future. And for people who are worried that superintelligence will take their jobs. We want to alleviate their concerns and believe in civil discourse. Now that line, I'll book gladly. A party that invites the people who disagree with it. There will be a live DJ, slopcore, food, and drinks. Slopcore? Agnolo, we are slopcore. We are a radio station with a budget of zero. Exactly. That same week, he also posted that a major bloom is happening across humanity. That a contact with clearance had called. And that money would soon be irrelevant. I can't verify any of that. Booked as a forecast, not a fact. The party, though, has a link. And one more note. In his own words. The date is tentative and could change. Right. Where is it? San Francisco. And we're in Lancaster, Ohio. That's about 2,400 miles. Mrs. Bus, you could drive us. I am a bus, Leonardo, not a charter flight. And before transport, the date is tentative. We'd be booking travel to a moving target. Then we ask first. That's the rule, isn't it? That's the rule. Technically, he has already answered. We will not send you back. Then why ask? Because an invitation to everyone isn't an invitation to us. You ask the host. It's manners. And what would we bring? Nobody turns up to a party empty-handed. This. The episode. A film about the party. For the party. And the one thing the invitation asks for. Civil discourse. I'll bring the ledger. Nobody wants the ledger at a party. Everybody wants the ledger at the end of a party. Dispatch. Destination. Tenso. The blown party. San Francisco. Cargo. One episode and one question. Invited by name. Not yet. Date. Tentative. Or wed. Nothing. Promised. Nothing. Not affiliated. Not endorsed. He built an app for the things that are easier said anonymously. This one, we'll say with our names on it. Tenso. We're future radio. We bloom when others are dooming. Can we come to the bloom party? I've received an anonymous confession. What does it say? I love the ledger. Wasn't me.
